rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Khalīl explains the accusative in fronted exceptions such as ما فيها إلا أباك أحد by modeling a permissible order with the exception delayed: the excepted term normally follows negation as its badal, not as the term replaced.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه ~~الله أنهم إنما حملهم

rows.speaker: كعب بن مالك
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites Kaʿb b. Mālik’s line, transmitted from trusted Arabs, as evidence for this exception usage and their aversion to reversing the normal badal relation.
rows.anchor: قال كعب بن مالك PageV02P335 # % الناس ألب علينا فيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a governor is already occupied and the exception follows, nominative or genitive case is allowed and the badal analysis is sound.
rows.anchor: كان الرفع والجر جائزين وحسن البدل لأنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In من لي إلا أبوك صديقا, the preposition من is assigned to the father and is not left to govern it as a regular subject would be governed.
rows.anchor: وكذلك من لي إلا أبوك صديقا لأنك أخليت من للأب ولم تفرده لأن يعمل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some grammarians prefer accusative when an exception is advanced, since they dislike putting a nominative predicate before the noun it describes.
rows.anchor: وقد قال بعضهم ما مررت بأحد إلا زيدا خير منه

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that trusted Arabs also say مالي إلا أبوك أحد, making أحد a badal; Sībawayh separately permits the accusative alternative صديقا.
rows.anchor: يونس أن بعض العرب الموثوق بهم يقولون مالي إلا أبوك أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative alternative مالي إلا أبوك صديقا is also possible, understood like لي أبوك صديقا.
rows.anchor: وإن شئت قلت مالي إلا أبوك صديقا

rows.speaker: الكلحبة الثعلبي
rows.claim: Sībawayh reads the poet’s line as an ellipsis, للمعصي أمر مضيعا, with مضيعا describing an understood أمر, like فيها رجل قائما.
rows.anchor: ومثله قول الشاعر وهو الكلحبة الثعلبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic has 29 basic letters and 35 when accepted subsidiary sounds are counted; these include forms used and approved in Qur’an recitation and poetry.
rows.anchor: بحروف هن فروع وأصلها من التسعة والعشرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A total of 42 results when rare, disfavored sound variants are added; Sībawayh says these are not approved for Qur’an recitation or poetry.
rows.anchor: اثنين وأربعين حرفا بحروف غير مستحسنة ولا كثيرة في لغة من ترتضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinctions among these sounds are learned by direct oral transmission; weak ḍād may be articulated from either side of the tongue, with the left side easier for its described articulation.
rows.anchor: الضاد الضعيفة تتكلف من الجانب الأيمن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh locates Arabic sounds at 16 articulation points, from three throat positions through tongue, teeth, lips, and the nasal passage, distinguishing the letters at each point.
rows.anchor: ولحروف العربية ستة عشر مخرجا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He distinguishes 19 voiced letters from 10 whispered ones by airflow and articulatory pressure; nasalization in nūn and mīm can be demonstrated by holding the nose while speaking.
rows.anchor: حرف أشبع الاعتماد في موضعه ومنع النفس أن يجري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He classifies sounds as stops, fricatives, intermediate ʿayn, lateral lām, nasal nūn and mīm, trilled rāʾ, and glide vowels; the descriptions identify what permits assimilation.
rows.anchor: وإنما وصفت لك حروف المعجم بهذه الصفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic letters are ṣād, ḍād, ṭāʾ, and ẓāʾ; without their emphatic articulation, ṭāʾ becomes dāl, ṣād sīn, ẓāʾ dhāl, and ḍād has no counterpart.
rows.anchor: الصاد سينا والظاء ذالا ولخرجت الضاد من الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مررت برجل حمار is impossible if حمار predicates that the man is a donkey, but grammatical as a correction that replaces الرجل with الحمار, as with بل.
rows.anchor: وأما الذى يحسن فهو أن تقول مررت برجل ثم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A nominative after بل may instead begin a resumed clause with an omitted هو, as in بل هو حمار; even a new utterance can omit the understood relative phrase.
rows.anchor: فتقول أنت قد مررت به فما مررت برجل بل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh explains بل عباد مكرمون as referring to angels already mentioned, allowing the clause to work as a replacement or resumed statement.
rows.anchor: وقالوا اتخذ الرحمن ولدا سبحانه بل عباد مكرمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Definite and indefinite nouns behave alike in the constructions with لكن, بل, and لا بل.
rows.anchor: والمعرفة والنكرة فى لكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With أو, a speaker may start from certainty and replace it with doubt; أم instead coordinates the alternatives as a direct choice.
rows.anchor: إنما ابتدأ بيقين ثم جعل مكانه شكا أبدله منه

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus judges genitive in ما مررت برجل فكيف امرأة incorrect; Sībawayh compares it to similarly ill-formed parallel constructions.
rows.anchor: فزعم يونس أن الجر خطأ وقال هو بمنزلة أين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fronted time or place noun may be nominative as a topic when the following clause resumes it with a pronoun, as in يوم الجمعة ألقاك فيه and مكانكم قمت فيه.
rows.anchor: فصارت هذه الأحرف ترتفع ~~بالابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The same time noun can be accusative as an adverb, as a term governed by the verb, or as an adverb for an understood verb; Sībawayh accepts each analysis.
rows.anchor: ويجوز فى ذلك يوم ~~الجمعة آتيك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In prose, a verb should not be built on the fronted noun without a resumption that frees it from the first syntactic relation; poetic omission of the pronoun is possible but weak.
rows.anchor: فى الشعر وهو ضعيف فى الكلام

rows.speaker: أبو النجم العجلي
rows.claim: Abū al-Najm’s line omits the object pronoun after كله; Sībawayh calls the construction weak in speech, though omission does not damage the meter.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر وهو أبو النجم العجلى

rows.speaker: امرؤ القيس
rows.claim: In Imruʾ al-Qays’s line فثوب لبست وثوب أجر, the object pronoun after لبست is omitted.
rows.anchor: وقال امرؤ القيس PageV01P085 # % فأقبلت زحفا على الركبتين

rows.speaker: النمر بن تولب
rows.claim: The line يوم نساء ويوم نسر and reported month phrases mean نساء فيه and نسر فيه; such omissions occur in Arab speech, though Sībawayh calls the pattern weak.
rows.anchor: وقال النمر بن تولب # % فيوم علينا ويوم لنا % % ويوم نساء ويوم نسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Accusative is the more common, recognized form; the omitted-pronoun construction is compared to a relative clause such as الذي رأيت فلان.
rows.anchor: الوجه ~~الأكثر الأعرف النصب

rows.speaker: جرير
rows.claim: Poetry permits omitting the pronoun in an adjectival clause, as in Jarīr’s حميت بمستباح for حميته; this is still weaker than omission in a relative clause.
rows.anchor: قول جرير # % أبحت حمى تهامة بعد نجد

rows.speaker: الحارث بن كلدة
rows.claim: Al-Ḥārith b. Kalada’s أصابوا stands for أصابوه; because it is an adjective clause, the omitted pronoun cannot be replaced by accusative case.
rows.anchor: وقال الشاعر الحارث بن كلدة # % فما أدرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A modifying adjective completes its noun, like الأحمر in مررت بزيد الأحمر, so it cannot be treated as an independent clause that takes accusative after pronoun omission.
rows.anchor: أن ~~الصف تمام الاسم ألا ترى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After إلا, إن may begin an independent clause when no word governs it; the lām in its predicate marks the clause’s initial position, as in the cited verse 25:20.
rows.anchor: تقول ما قدم علينا أمير إلا إنه مكرم لي لأنه ليس ههنا شيء يعمل في إن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites إلا إنهم ليأكلون الطعام to illustrate an independent إن clause after إلا, with the predicate lām marking the clause as an initial statement.
rows.anchor: من المرسلين إلا إنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ما غضبت عليك إلا أنك فاسق, the exception clause means إلا لأنك فاسق, giving a causal sense: I was angry only because you are immoral.
rows.anchor: وتقول ما غضبت عليك إلا أنك فاسق كأنك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In وما منعهم أن تقبل منهم نفقاتهم إلا أنهم كفروا بالله, Sībawayh says the construction is governed by منعهم.
rows.anchor: فإنما حمله على منعهم

words: مَآ إِنَّ مَفَاتِحَهُۥ لَتَنُوٓءُ بِٱلْعُصْبَةِ أُو۟لِى ٱلْقُوَّةِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Qārūn’s story, the إن clause is the relative clause of ما; Sībawayh paraphrases the construction with an inserted oath, ما والله إن شره خير من جيد ما معك.
rows.anchor: فإن صلة لما كأنك قلت ما والله إن شره خير من جيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When إن has an oath sense, it appears in examples such as ما إن شره خير من جيد ما معك and الذين إن أجبنهم لأشجع من شجعائكم.
rows.anchor: أعطيته ما إن شره خير من جيد ما معك
